newsitem.title: USA: Arbitrage rules saving Treasury a bundle-economist.
newsitem.headline: Arbitrage rules saving Treasury a bundle-economist.

text.p: The arbitrage rebate rules that Congress enacted in 1986 have reduced the amount of tax-exempt bonds outstanding considerably -- saving the federal government in 1993 alone about $1 billion, a Treasury Department economist has reported.

"The arbitrage rules alone appear to have reduced the amount of tax-exempt bonds outstanding (in 1993) by about an additional $50 billion and avoided a revenue loss of about $1 billion," Bruce Davie, financial economist in Treasury's office of tax analysis, said in the 20-page report.
Davie conceded that the federal government's complex arbitrage rules are a "constant source of irritation" to states and localities.
Issuer groups have made many suggestions for relaxing some of the rules and simplifying others, he said.

But absent radical tax reform, such as enacting a consumption tax or other major unlikely reforms, "arbitrage rules are necessary to prevent runaway erosion of the income tax base through the issuance of tax-exempt bonds," Davie said.
He noted that his findings are his own and not necessarily those of Treasury.
Davie said that the tax-exempt bond provisions of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 are probaby best known for the volume cap imposed on most private activity bonds.

That and other curbs in the law have reduced the volume of tax-exempt bonds currently outstanding, and the resulting revenue loss to the federal government, by some "large, but unknowable, amount," Davie said.

In addition to the volume cap, Davie was referring to Congress' decisions in 1986 to bar issuance of pension bonds, to limit governmental and 501(c)(3) issues to one advance refunding, and to cap amounts outstanding for nonhospital purposes for any one 501(c)(3) entity to $150 million.
